title: The Register of the Gods
subtitle: Hierarchical Clustering · hclust + cutree + summarise
story: You are an apprentice to the keeper at the Temple of the Gods. The keeper died of a fever last month and with him were lost two important registers: which offering each shrine takes, and which god each shrine serves. According to custom, a temple whose keeper dies is closed forever — its fires never relit — unless the registers exist. You have until midday, when the sun is at its zenith and the shafts of light through the roof stand straight and touch the altar, to rebuild them. The evidence is still here — the residues in every vessel, the figures standing in every niche. Rebuild both registers, light the ring of fires at the altar so the temple is seen to be kept, and then cross the canopy bridge to the temple beyond and tell them the registers are in hand.

done.title: The practical register is whole
done.body: Every shrine, every offering, in your own hand — and two of them filed against the stone in the inner vault, because the vessels said so and the stone was only recording where things happen to stand. It is the smaller of the two books and the easier one. Outside, the shadow under the parapet has pulled in almost to nothing.

escapeDone.title: Not closed
escapeDone.body: Three groups, and the last one closes. Whatever the figures in those niches have been saying to each other for four hundred years, you have finally heard it. You tip the one flame you carried up out of the dark into the channel and it runs the whole ring, basin to basin, with the sun standing straight overhead and the whole green roof of the forest flat below. He taught you after all — he just did it by leaving everything exactly where it was.

worldPlatePrompt: A world-bible establishing plate for a LIVING, KEPT jungle temple, deep in rainforest, at harsh equatorial midday. This sanctuary was tended every day until a month ago, when its keeper died: it is swept, maintained and in use — NOT a ruin. Nothing has collapsed, there is no rubble, nothing is growing through the floor, and the forest is cut hard back and stops at the wall. One frame holding the whole world's vocabulary: massive warm honey-and-ochre limestone masonry, close-jointed and clean, its carved faces still crisp and still holding traces of painted plaster; a gallery of shallow shrine niches cut along the wall, each hung with a single banner of strong flat colour; small carved stone and clay votive figures standing in tidy rows on wiped niche ledges; lamps with trimmed wicks and shallow offering bowls set square before them, recently used and now cold; stoppered resin jars stacked in order along the floor; a low rough service crawl-way cut behind the wall at floor level — the one unfinished thing, its dust worn into a smooth path by daily passing; and hard white shafts of sunlight falling straight down through openings in the canopy far above, striking the floor in sharp bright pools. LIGHT: harsh, flat and OVERHEAD, high noon, hard-edged shafts and short shadows. Deliberately NOT golden hour, NOT dusk, NOT dawn, NOT lamplit — no warm amber wash anywhere, no firelight, no brass glow. PALETTE: RICH AND LUMINOUS, not grey and not washed-out — warm honey stone, deep wet greens in the forest beyond, real blue in the sky and in the shadows, clear water. The nine banners are the only PURE, fully saturated colour in the frame and nothing else competes with them for chroma, but everything else is still full of colour and light. Humid air, drifting spore and dust in the light shafts, water beading on stone. Painterly, cinematic, subtle film grain. question.prompt: He drew for sister shrines from a single jar, so the offering laid down at Ninestep is kin to the offering at exactly one other shrine. Which shrine is it?

feedback.correct: Correct — noted: Ninestep's nearest kin is Longshadow.
wrong: Every shrine is six numbers. Two shrines are kin when those six sets of numbers sit closest together — so measure the distance from Ninestep to each of the others.
`dist()` on the six residue columns gives you every pairwise distance at once; read the row for Ninestep and take its smallest entry.
Three shrines sit close to Ninestep and five sit far away. Among the close three, one is clearly nearer than the rest — that is the sister, not merely a near neighbour.
